opus-5.5.text:
I think generalization for agents is the hardest open problem right now, and the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet. But there are a few directions I believe in.

First, the base model matters more than people sometimes assume. A lot of agent capability is downstream of the pretrained model's general reasoning and world knowledge. If the base model is weak, you end up patching behavior task by task, and that never generalizes. So continuing to scale pretraining, and improving the quality and diversity of data, is still foundational.

Second, reinforcement learning has to move beyond narrow, well-defined environments. Today much of agent RL happens in settings with clean, verifiable rewards, like coding or math, where you can check whether the answer is right. That's a good starting point, but real-world tasks are messy: goals are ambiguous, feedback is delayed, and there's often no single correct answer. To generalize, we need many more environments and much more diverse tasks, and we need ways to get reward signals for things that aren't easily verifiable. That could mean better reward models, using the model itself as a judge, or learning from human feedback in more scalable ways.

Third, I think long-horizon capability is key. A general agent has to plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and keep context coherent over many steps. A lot of current failures aren't about lacking knowledge; the model drifts, forgets what it was doing, or can't correct itself. Training directly on long trajectories, and letting the model learn from its own failures during RL, helps a lot here.

And finally, there's a balance between specialization and generality. It's tempting to optimize hard for a benchmark or one product scenario, and you get quick gains. But if you overfit to specific tools or formats, the model becomes brittle. Our view is that you want the model to learn the underlying skills, like reasoning, exploration, and tool use as a general behavior, rather than memorizing workflows. If you get that right, transfer to new tasks starts to emerge naturally, much like we saw with language models generalizing across domains after pretraining.

So in short: a strong base model, more diverse and realistic environments, better reward signals for open-ended tasks, and training for long-horizon behavior. I think that combination is how agents go from impressive demos to something genuinely general.

fable-5.1.text:
I think generalization for agents really comes down to one thing: the model has to learn the underlying capability, not the specific task. A lot of what we see today is models that look very good on one benchmark, one environment, one set of tools, and then you move them slightly outside that distribution and they break. That's not an agent, that's a script with a language model inside it.

So the way I think about it, there are a few layers.

The first is the training signal. If you do reinforcement learning on a narrow set of environments, you get a narrow agent. The model learns to exploit the structure of those particular tasks. To get generalization you need diversity in environments — coding, browsing, tool use, long-horizon planning, things with very different reward structures — and you need the model to be rewarded for the process of solving problems, not just for memorizing solutions. Scaling the number and variety of environments is, in my view, as important as scaling parameters was in the pretraining era.

The second is that pretraining and RL are not separate things. People sometimes talk as if you pretrain a base model and then "add agent capabilities" on top. I think that's the wrong mental model. The base model's world knowledge, its reasoning, its ability to read documentation it has never seen and figure out an API — that's the foundation of generalization. RL sharpens and aligns that; it doesn't create it from nothing. So a stronger, more general base model will always produce a more general agent.

The third is long context and memory. A generalizable agent has to be able to operate in a new situation by reading, exploring, and accumulating state, rather than relying on having seen that exact situation in training. That means the model needs to use context very efficiently — to pull in a codebase, a long conversation, a set of tool outputs, and actually reason over all of it coherently. If context is short or the model loses track, you're forced to hard-code things, and hard-coding is the enemy of generalization.

And then the fourth, which is maybe more philosophical: the agent has to be able to learn from its own experience. Right now most of the learning happens before deployment. A truly general agent should get better at a task while doing it, through self-reflection, verification, trying things and observing outcomes. That's where I think a lot of the next few years' progress will come from — closing the loop between acting in the world and updating the model.

So if I summarize: diverse environments, a strong general base, long-horizon context, and learning from experience. If you get those four right, I think the agent stops being a demo and starts being something you can actually hand new problems to.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to move from learning how to solve a particular task to learning how to interact with an environment. An agent needs to understand what information it’s missing, take an action, observe the result, and adjust its approach. Those abilities should transfer across tasks, even when the tools or the interface change.

To get there, we need diversity in training—not just more examples of the same workflow, but different environments, goals, and kinds of feedback. Otherwise, it’s very easy for a model to memorize a sequence of actions without learning why those actions work. Reinforcement learning can help, but the training setup has to reward achieving the goal, rather than following a particular path.

I also think generalization depends on the underlying model’s reasoning ability. You can’t anticipate every situation an agent will encounter. It needs to use what it already knows to work through something unfamiliar, recognize when it has made a mistake, and recover. So I’d focus on stronger base models, more diverse interactive training, and evaluations that actually test unfamiliar situations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to move from learning specific workflows to learning how to solve problems across different environments. If an agent is trained mostly on a fixed set of tools and tasks, it can become very good at those tasks, but struggle when the interface changes or when it encounters a problem that requires a different strategy.

So we need both more diverse training environments and a way to learn from the outcomes of longer interactions. The model needs to practice exploring, making mistakes, recovering, and checking whether it actually accomplished the goal. The training signal should reward that ability, rather than just reproducing a particular sequence of actions.

And evaluation matters here. We should test on new tools, new environments, and new combinations of familiar capabilities. That helps distinguish whether the agent has learned a reusable problem-solving strategy or simply memorized a workflow. My intuition is that generalization will come from combining a strong foundation model with this kind of broad, interactive training.
